sections.html:
In Allegheny County the Division of Real Estate does the recorder’s work. It is in Room 101 of the County Office Building, 542 Forbes Avenue, Pittsburgh, and it also collects the state and local transfer taxes.

The counter is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Phone 412-350-4636 and choose Option 2. Most documents can be eRecorded online, so a title company in another city can submit a deed without anyone walking into Room 101.

Most sellers never visit the counter. The title agent prepares the deed, records it, and sends the tax and fee payments the division requires.

A deed costs $200.00 to record, and so does a mortgage, under the schedule effective January 1, 2026. Large documents add charges only when they pass 30 parcels or 30 indexed names.

Allegheny County recording fees effective January 1, 2026
Document typeStandard fee
Deed and deed related documents$200.00
Mortgage and mortgage related documents$200.00
Power of attorney$50.00
Notary public bond and commission$80.00
Financial statement$175.00
Military service dischargeNo fee

Each parcel past 30 on a deed adds $10.00, and each indexed name past 30 adds $5.00. Deed related documents include leases, rights of way, declarations of trust, oil and gas documents and sewage permits, all at the same $200.00.

The tax runs from 2% to 5% of the price depending on where the house is, and 1% of that goes to the state. The rest goes to the municipality and the school district that cover the property.

The division collects every layer at recording, with one check for transfer tax and a second check for the recording fee. The county’s own examples show the spread:

  • A house in Shaler Township pays 1% to the state, 0.5% to the township and 0.5% to Shaler Area School District, for 2% in total.
  • A house in the City of Pittsburgh pays 1% to the state, 3% to the city and 1% to Pittsburgh School District, for 5% in total.

On a real sale that gap is large, so ask the closing agent for the exact municipal and school rates before the settlement statement is final.

When no price appears on the deed, or when an exemption applies, a Statement of Value on Pennsylvania form REV-183 is required. Certain family transfers can skip the form if the deed carries a sentence explaining the relationship. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, at 717-783-8104, handles exemption questions.

Type the deed in black ink on white or manila sheets, 8 1/2 by 11 inches or 8 1/2 by 14 inches, in a font of at least 10 points. Continuous paper is rejected.

  • Leave a one inch margin at the top of the first page for the certification stamp.
  • Print a name and a full address with zip code in the Record and Mail to area, outside that top margin.
  • Handwriting is limited to signatures, acknowledgments and a few listed exceptions.
  • Keep out tape, glue, staples, correction fluid and highlighting.
  • Double-sided pages are fine, though each side that carries text counts as a separate page for the fee.

The Certificate of Residence has its own formatting rule, and the county publishes content requirements for each document type separately.

In person, the counter takes cash, a business check, a money order or a cashier’s check. Personal checks, debit cards and credit cards are refused.

Firms that record often can open a draw down account in the office during business hours, which saves a trip with a check each time. Online payment is available for eRecorded filings, and the county posts a separate sheet for copies and their fees.

If you see an unfamiliar deed or mortgage filed against your property, the county has a web form for reporting suspected deed or mortgage fraud.

sections.h2: Common level ratio and your deed
sections.html:
The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue issues a new Common Level Ratio factor for each county every year, effective July 1, and the Division of Real Estate links to it from its transfer tax page. It sits beside the Statement of Value, so a filer working on a gift or low-price deed sees both together.

The county’s appeal board uses 49.3% as the ratio for the 2027 tax year. A figure near 49% tells you that county assessments, frozen to a 2012 base year, run well below current market prices. Ask the closing agent which figure belongs on the Statement of Value before you sign the deed.

The county covers 745 square miles, and the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet at Downtown Pittsburgh to form the Ohio. With 130 municipalities, it has more local governments than any other county in Pennsylvania, and neighboring municipalities can carry different transfer tax rates.

Population is 1,225,035 as of July 2025, with 614,484 housing units. About 65.2% of homes are owner-occupied, and the median value of an owner-occupied home is $227,600. Roughly 35% of units are renter occupied, which matters when you own a duplex or a house with tenants in place.

sections.h2: Checklist before the deed is recorded
sections.html:
1. Confirm the municipality and school district, since those two set most of the transfer tax.
  2. Review the deed against the formatting rules above so the division does not reject it.
  3. Decide who pays transfer tax. Grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for it, so settle the split in writing.
  4. Choose eRecording or hand delivery, and for hand delivery plan on a business check, cashier’s check, money order or cash.

Buyers of rental houses have a second step. Under Act 29 of 2026, a new owner of non-owner-occupied real estate must send contact details to the county’s chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a knowingly false filing can bring a fine of up to $500. If you are handing a tenant-occupied house to an investor, you can mention that duty to the buyer.

sections.h2: What a cash sale changes at the counter
sections.html: Nothing about the recording changes when the buyer pays cash. The deed still needs correct formatting, a transfer tax check and a fee check. What goes away is the lender’s paperwork, so your closing may move faster. If you still have a mortgage, ask your title agent to confirm the payoff and the recording of the release so the public record is clean afterward.

faqs.q: What is the standard recording fee for a deed in Allegheny County?
faqs.a: It is $200.00 for a deed and for a mortgage under the fee sheet effective January 1, 2026. Parcels beyond 30 add $10.00 each and indexed names beyond 30 add $5.00 each.

faqs.q: Does Allegheny County take personal checks or cards at the recording counter?
faqs.a: No. The Division of Real Estate does not accept personal checks, debit cards or credit cards. It takes cash, business checks, money orders, cashier's checks and draw down accounts, and online payment exists for eRecorded filings.

faqs.q: Why is the transfer tax so different between Pittsburgh and the suburbs?
faqs.a: The 1% state share is constant, while the municipal and school district shares change by location. Shaler Township totals 2% and the City of Pittsburgh totals 5%.

faqs.q: Can a deed be recorded without visiting Room 101?
faqs.a: Yes, most documents can be eRecorded online. For hand delivery, the address is 542 Forbes Avenue, Room 101, and the counter keeps weekday hours.

faqs.q: Does a military discharge cost anything to record in Allegheny County?
faqs.a: No. Military service discharge papers, street or alley vacations and ordinances are listed with no recording fee.
